articles.title: Google Search charged with breaking EU antitrust rules
articles.summary: Google is violating the DMA by favoring its own search services over rival comparison providers, according to the European Commission.
articles.body: Google is breaking European antitrust laws by favoring its own Shopping, Hotels, and Flights search services over rival comparison providers, according to the European Commission. The EU announced in its preliminary ruling today that Google’s parent company, Alphabet, had also violated anti-steering rules under the Digital Markets Act (DMA) by preventing app developers on its Play Store from steering customers to other distribution channels. Google can challenge the preliminary charges or make additional compliance changes ahead of the EU’s final ruling. The EU can fine companies up to 10 percent of their global annual revenue for DMA violations, which would be a maximum of $35 billion based on the $350 billion Alphabet earned in 2024. “In the first case, our preliminary view is that Alphabet is in breach of the Digital Markets Act by favouring its own products on the Google Search results page, which means suppliers and competitors do not benefit from fair ranking practices,” Teresa Ribera, European executive vice president for clean, just, and competitive transition, says in a statement. Google believes the changes Europe is pushing for in search are “misguided,” Oliver Bethell, Google’s senior director of competition, writes in a blog post. Bethell warns, for example, that if Google “can’t show travel results that take people directly to airline sites, they typically end up with a more expensive ticket because airlines have to pay commissions to intermediary websites.” He also says the changes have led to traffic declines of up to 30 percent for some businesses. When it comes to Google’s mobile app store, the EU believes that “Alphabet does not effectively allow Android phone users to be told about or directed to cheaper offers from app developers outside the Google Play store,” Ribera says. Bethell says the commission’s findings on app distribution “create a false choice between openness and security.” He says the government “is effectively forcing us to choose between a closed model” — more similar to Apple’s iOS, which requires apps to be reviewed before distribution — “and an unsafe one,” where Google is forced to give users access to “scammy or malicious links that take our users outside of the secure Play environment.” Europe’s EVP for tech sovereignty, security, and democracy, Henna Virkkunen, says that “both practices negatively impact many European and non-European businesses that rely on Google Search or Google Play to reach their users in the EU. Ensuring that Alphabet fully complies with the DMA is key to ensure business and innovation opportunities for all providers of digital services.” The announcement comes after the EU opened an investigation into Google Search on March 25th over concerns that it was treating its own services more favorably in Search’s ranking than services provided by third-party rivals — something the EU fined the company €2.4 billion (worth about $2.5 billion today) for doing with Google Shopping in 2017. Apple was the first company to be charged under the DMA in June 2024, and soon after, Meta was hit with a preliminary ruling that its advertising model also violates the act. Google had introduced several changes to its Search services in a bid to comply with new DMA rules. These included adding new search result layouts that boosted links to third-party comparison websites and removing the Google Flights widget for Search users in the EU. It even tested a decluttered return to the classic 10 blue links. The DMA targets specific “gatekeepers” — companies that provide core digital services to European consumers — requiring them to allow more interoperability and avoid giving their own digital services preferential treatment. Alphabet was designated as a gatekeeper in September 2023, with a compliance deadline of March 6th, 2024. The ruling follows rising tensions between European policymakers and US President Donald Trump, who has surrounded himself with fawning US tech CEOs who have criticized fines placed on them by the EU as a form of taxation. The Financial Times reported in January that an increase in US pressure was allegedly leading the EU to soften its approach to big tech regulation and reassess its investigations into Apple, Meta, and Google.

articles.title: Google hit with $1 billion fine for breaking EU antitrust rules
articles.summary: The fine follows a two year DMA investigation into Google’s Search and Play Store policies, which will now have to change.
articles.body: The European Union has fined Google’s parent company Alphabet €890 million (about $1 billion) for two separate violations of the bloc’s Digital Markets Act (DMA). One penalty is for giving its own products preferential treatment in search results, while the other is for blocking Android developers from sending users to alternate payment options. A €460 million fine has been issued to Google for giving preferential treatment to its own Shopping, Hotels, and Flights services in Google Search results. The second €430 million penalty is for Play Store rules preventing developers from freely steering consumers to alternative payment systems that may be cheaper. As part of the ruling, Google has been given 60 days to make changes to its policies, or face further periodic penalty payments. In Search, it will be required to treat third-party services “in a fair and non-discriminatory manner,” while it will also have to allow Android developers to freely promote offers to users both inside and outside the Play Store. The fines were announced by the European Commission today, more than two years after it first opened a non-compliance investigation, and follow a preliminary ruling in March 2025. Google was given time to address the EU’s concerns, with an extension granted in May 2026 after the Commission said a previous proposal from the company “is simply not ​strong enough.” Google made and tested several changes to its Search services in an effort to comply with DMA rules, such as removing the Google Flights widget for Search users in the EU, and boosting links to third-party comparison websites via an updated search result layout. The company has previously fired back at the EU’s criticisms of its Search product, telling Reuters in May that changes it made in an attempt to achieve DMA compliance “represent the ​biggest downgrade in the product’s history, creating a ​second-rate experience ⁠for Europeans to the benefit of a few self-interested complainants.” These changes were made prior to Google introducing a reimagined AI-focused search box at its I/O conference in May, however, which has also rolled out to EU users. Google was previously hit with a €2.42 billion fine in 2017 for a similar breach of the EU’s antitrust rules, after it was charged with giving its comparison shopping service an illegal advantage over competitors. As for the Play Store, Google has repeatedly objected to rules requiring it to open up app distribution on Android systems, claiming doing so poses a security risk to users. The company repeated these objections following the Commission’s preliminary finding and in a blog posted last year, said “the DMA is making it difficult to protect users from scams and malicious links on Android by forcing us to remove our legitimate safeguards that protect users’ security and safety.” Nevertheless, it updated certain terms following consultations with the European Commission and other experts, revising fees and restrictions on Android developers. The Commission says these changes “constitute good progress towards compliance.” Google is also facing a reckoning over its Play Store policies in the US after Fortnite publisher Epic Games successfully sued the company over in-app purchase fees, and it will be forced to carry rival Android app stores inside its own. The DMA targets the largest “gatekeeper” companies that provide core digital services in Europe, and requires them to act in a fair manner — not stifle competition by abusing their market dominance. The maximum fine for breaching DMA rules is 10 percent of the company’s global annual revenue — $40 billion in Google’s case, based on the $400 billion it reported for 2025. “The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine,” says Teresa Ribera, the Commission’s executive vice-president for clean, just and competitive transition. “And European consumers have a right to be told by app developers where to sign up to the best offers, even when the app store owner does not get a cut. This is the promise of the DMA, protecting fairness, choice and innovation in digital markets for the benefit of all European citizens.”

articles.title: Japan’s Wages Grow Most Since 1997, Keeping BOJ on Rate Hike Path
articles.summary: Japanese workers’ nominal wages rose at the fastest pace in nearly three decades on the back of strong corporate earnings and a tight labor market, in data l...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Japanese workers' nominal wages rose at the fastest pace in nearly three decades on the back of strong corporate earnings and a tight labor market, in data likely to keep the Bank of Japan on course for further monetary tightening.

Nominal pay climbed 4.7% in July from a year earlier, following a revised 4% increase in June, the labor ministry reported Tuesday. The gain, the biggest since 1997, far exceeded economists' forecast of 3.8% and marked a sixth straight month in which the advance exceeded 3%, the longest such streak in 34 years.

Real wages — adjusted for inflation excluding rents — gained 2.4%, marking the largest gain in about five years. Base pay also advanced 4.1%, while a more stable measure — which strips out bonuses and overtime and sampling distortions — rose 2.7% for full-time workers.

The stronger-than-expected figures bolster the case for the BOJ to proceed with a widely expected rate hike this month. Markets have largely priced in a move when the board meets next week, with some investors expecting further tightening after a relatively short interval.

The BOJ's ability to sustain that tightening path will depend in part on whether rising incomes translate into stronger domestic demand. For now, there is reason for doubt. Data last week showed that household spending fell for an eighth consecutive month in July, as shoppers cut back on discretionary outlays. That was after gross domestic product data for the second quarter showed that private consumption flatlined in the period.

The wage gains are partly the result of another strong round of annual wage negotiations, through which workers at companies under the Rengo union umbrella secured pay gains of more than 5% for a third year. Separately, the national minimum wage for the current fiscal year climbed to an average of ¥1,177 ($7.55) per hour in what was the second-largest increase on record, suggesting that momentum is spreading across a broader range of workers and industries.

Healthy corporate profits have helped companies shoulder higher labor costs. Current profits rose for a seventh consecutive quarter in the three months through June, led by manufacturers amid booming demand related to artificial intelligence and data centers.

articles.title: LG TVs caught spying even when offline or on standby
articles.summary: Gamers Nexus gives you another reason to never connect your smart TV to the internet.
articles.body: LG smart TVs are almost constantly logging and uploading data about owners and their homes, even when offline or on standby mode, according to a new report from YouTube channel Gamers Nexus. The company’s TV sets scan Wi-Fi networks for nearby devices, record audio logs through their microphones, and use audio and video sampling to recognize exactly what you’re watching from across the TV inputs. Gamers Nexus partnered with fellow YouTubers Level1Techs and independent security researchers for the investigation, which involved testing retail LG OLEDs. Packet captures showed the TVs scanning the local area network for nearby hardware like phones or smartwatches, as well as logging location data and details of nearby Wi-Fi networks, and feeding the information back to LG Ad Solutions. Perhaps more concerningly, the TVs were capable of recording microphone audio when in standby; this continued even after the TV was disconnected from the internet, with audio files stored offline and uploaded once a connection was restored. [Media: The final piece of the puzzle is Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), tech that uses audio and video data to figure out what you’re actually watching, examining the apps you use through the TV’s own smart interface and the content you connect via HDMI and other ports. ACR isn’t just an LG issue though: A new video from RTINGS digs into how ACR is used by almost every smart TV manufacturer to figure out what you watch. This isn’t LG’s first brush with Gamers Nexus. In July this year, the channel flagged that some LG monitors were automatically installing an app that collected device data and ran pop-up ads for LG’s other apps and even McAfee antivirus. The public pressure from that video prompted an intervention from Microsoft, and ultimately led to LG disabling the pop-up ads.

articles.title: GLP-1 prescriptions for kids up more than 30,000 percent since 2019
articles.summary: Kids with obesity-related conditions like high cholesterol or sleep apnea were substantially more likely to be prescribed GLP-1s than those without.
articles.body:
NewsNation — Over the last seven years, GLP-1 medication use in children age 8 to 11 has increased by nearly 31,000 percent, according to a new NYU Langone Health study .

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved any GLP-1 medication for children under 12, but in drastic circumstances, doctors have prescribed it off-label.

Researchers analyzed health records for 3,520,531 children with obesity but without diabetes. The share of those children ages 8 to 11 who were prescribed a GLP-1 rose from 0.03 percent in 2019 to 9.3 percent in 2026 — a 310-fold increase. Kids with obesity-related conditions , from high cholesterol to sleep apnea, were substantially more likely to be prescribed the drugs than those without.

Dr. Babak J. Orandi, the study’s lead investigator and associate professor in the Departments of Surgery and Medicine at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, told the New York Post that despite the sharp rise, only 0.6 percent of the study’s 3.5 million children ever received a GLP-1 prescription over the full study period.

“In context, this is a very small number,” Orandi says. “Against that denominator, 20,282 GLP-1 children receiving prescriptions represents a tiny fraction of children eligible for treatment. While the number receiving treatment is very small, uptake is accelerating quickly.”

The doctor added that he is more concerned about the “underlying factors” driving obesity, which affects roughly 1 in 5 American children.

Overall, the study found that the weight loss drugs so far seem to be reserved “for those at greatest cardiometabolic risk.” Socioeconomic status also plays a role, with upper-income children more likely to be prescribed. Orandi notes, however, that “most who could benefit still aren’t.”

images.caption: GLP-1 medication use in children age 8 to 11 has increased by nearly 31,000%, according to a new NYU Langone Health study. (Photo by: Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images; Gareth Fuller/PA Images)

articles.title: The Movement: Vance faces pressure over Carlson friendship
articles.summary: Vice President Vance is in hot water with some conservatives after a press briefing last week where he defended his friendship with Tucker Carlson. “Tucker is a friend of mine,” Vance said. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things. And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance is in hot water with some conservatives after a press briefing last week where he defended his friendship with Tucker Carlson.

“Tucker is a friend of mine,” Vance said. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things. And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them.”

Carlson has been a divisive figure within the conservative movement. As an independent commentator, he has embraced people and ideas that run counter to many conservative values, especially in criticizing Israel and flirting with alternative theories about World War II. The divide within the GOP over Carlson still has fracture lines from last winter, when a slew of Heritage Foundation staff and trustees left the organization when its president defended Carlson for interviewing someone who had espoused antisemitic views.

Carlson has also been taking fire from many in the conservative movement as he has turned further against President Trump amid the war with Iran. Last week, Carlson said that left-wing Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was “ literally Trumpian ” and that he wouldn’t vote for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, the Trump-endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), “at gunpoint.”

Vance has been pressed repeatedly on his relationship with Carlson in recent months, including at a summit of Jewish Republican donors in Las Vegas last week. Although Vance reportedly tried to reassure the attendees that he was staunchly opposed to antisemitism, some were left unsatisfied with his response to questions on his friendship with Carlson.

At the press briefing a few days later, Vance was once again asked about, and once again did not denounce, Carlson.

“Everybody knows that Tucker Carlson and I are friends, and I think it’s very obvious that Tucker has said some things that I disagree with,” Vance said at the briefing. He added that El-Sayed is “a crazy person.”

That answer further riled up conservatives of all stripes.

“It’s one thing to say I’m not going to torch a friend, a personal friendship, as a result of a difference of opinions. I think that that sounds halfway reasonable because it is in a vacuum a reasonable thing to say,” said Stephanie Slade , an editor at Reason Magazine and author of a new book about the conservative movement. “But when you are the vice president of the United States and the person you’re talking about is one of the most popular podcasters on planet Earth, you do have an obligation to make sure the people who are looking to you as an example know whether you endorse exactly what you disagree with when you say you have disagreements with somebody, you know, what do you disagree with them about and why, and he is clearly avoiding committing himself on that because he does not want to alienate Tucker’s fans.”

Ben Shapiro , in a post on social media , said much the same. He referenced a December quote from Vance, when the vice president apparently said the idea that Carlson “has no place in the conservative movement” is “absurd.” Shapiro called for Vance to further articulate which views of Carlson’s are welcome in the movement, and which are not.

“So, the real question is that: does the VP still think that? If so, why? Why, precisely, are Tucker Carlson’s views — El-Sayed as ‘America First,’ Trump as anti-Christ, feudalism as superior to our current system, propagandizing on behalf of shariah law and Russia, anti-Semitic conspiracism, etc. — a part of the conservative movement?” Shapiro wrote.

Slade noted that Shapiro has been “on the front line” of a conservative pushback against antisemitism and white nationalism within the movement, which, she said, more and more people are denouncing.

“I do think there are some dominoes sort of falling here of people on the right who didn’t really realize just where the MAGA energy was going, especially among young people, and are starting to finally wake up to that,” Slade said.

The Hill reached out to Vance for comment. Others, however, are defending Vance’s right to be friends with Carlson and pointing out that the vice president clarified he disagreed with Carlson’s comments about El-Sayed and criticisms of Trump.

Sam Markstein, a spokesperson for the Republican Jewish Coalition, which hosted the summit earlier in the week, told The Jerusalem Post at the time that Vance “gave a good answer as to where he draws those lines and what those differences are.”

Mark Halperin , a conservative political commentator, suggested on his own show on Sept. 3 that people calling for Vance to fully denounce Tucker as a person were unreasonable.

“I can think of people I know who had grandparents who were racist. Does that mean you don’t love your grandparents?” Halperin said. “I mean, [Vance is] friends with Tucker, they have a friendship that’s based on, you know, all the things friendships are based on. And yet there’s this expectation that he should denounce his friend, beyond just saying where he disagrees with him? I guess I don’t understand the value system that says the vice president has to denounce his friend.”

But Philip Klein , editor of National Review, said the criticism Vance is receiving for his comments on Carlson, both at the Jewish Republicans’ gathering and in the briefing, is justified because he has not distanced himself adequately from Carlson’s antisemitism specifically. That’s especially a hot topic as the debate over Israel threatens to define the 2028 presidential race in both parties.

“At a time of historic levels of antisemitism in America, when the Democratic Party has already been consumed by antisemitism, a lot of people are genuinely worried about whether Republicans will move in the same direction,” Klein wrote. “It is completely legitimate to parse what Vance is saying on this subject.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes , Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

NOT ALL ARE HAPPY WITH WHITE HOUSE IDEA TO PAY STAY-AT-HOME PARENTS

Conservatives — and many others — are buzzing online about a new proposal from the White House that would allow stay-at-home parents to collect childcare subsidies.

Many family-focused conservatives see it as a win for making it easier for parents to raise their children. Others, though, call it a financially unhealthy kind of social welfare.

The split reflects a broader tension within the movement over government involvement in Americans’ lives. Vice President Vance , among others, has championed using federal incentives to encourage traditional family formation. Conservatives from the limited-government school of thought would prefer a more hands-off approach led by individual families.

The New York Times first reported the existence of the proposed rule change, which has been a priority for groups like the Heritage Foundation since before Trump took office. Roger Severino , a vice president for domestic policy at Heritage, wrote on social media that the Trump administration’s plan is similar to what Heritage had been pushing for and commended the proposal.

“Parents who hand their kids to commercial day care get subsidy payments, while parents who bear the toil, expense, and opportunity cost of raising their kids at home currently get ZERO. It’s illogical and unjust and this proposal would level the playing field,” Severino said.

“Critically, the stay at home benefit for two-parent households would be specifically tied to marriage because of course it should. Our government provides better treatment to marriage all over law and policy because marriage, on average, provides better treatment to kids.”

Critics sniped at the proposal, saying it would expand entitlement spending and comparing it to other countries that have tried and failed federal marriage-and-family incentive programs, like Hungary.

Dana Loesch, a conservative commentator, torched the proposal on the social platform X, calling it “welfare” and a “socialist program.” She said it was an example of “why the GOP has always been bifurcated.”

“People don’t need a nanny state to pay others to mind their own children — and the idea that we’re supposed to shut up and accept this makegood in lieu of ending runaway spending and lowering taxes so people can keep their own money for their own childcare instead of receiving handouts — is an insulting lie,” Loesch said.

GERMAN FAR-RIGHT PARTY BACKED BY US CONSERVATIVES MAKES GAINS

The Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, won big in a regional election in Germany over the weekend, showing that support for right-wing ideas, especially opposition to migration, is still surging in Europe.

Although AfD did not manage to win a majority that would allow them to govern the state of Saxony-Anhalt, the election showed that voters are enthusiastic for a platform resembling the American MAGA movement, and that AfD is closer than ever to overcoming mainstream parties’ opposition to working with them.

The election comes as conservatives in the U.S. look for influence in Western Europe, where many more moderate elected officials, like German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , have pushed back against the Trump administration over its war in Iran. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have criticized the mainstream parties for refusing to work with AfD and for labeling them “extremists,” and AfD leaders have forged ties with the MAGA movement more broadly over recent years. The lead AfD candidate, Ulrich Siegmund , publicly thanked Elon Musk for his support after Musk appeared to congratulate the AfD on Sunday.

The Trump administration is also reportedly planning to spend $4 million through the State Department to boost right-wing media in Europe, according to Reuters .

The goal is to “plan the restoration of America’s industrial independence,” with a focus on tech and AI. Details here .

articles.title: Chinese hackers are running AI on stolen networks to avoid detection, Google says
articles.summary: One China-linked group targets academic, medical and military AI research, the report says.
articles.body: Hackers working for Chinese intelligence are increasingly targeting American AI research and using AI in their operations, Google said Tuesday. In its latest quarterly report, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group said that several hacker groups, including both intelligence agencies and cybercrime gangs, have moved from basic AI prompting to using AI agents that automate wide swaths of their intrusion. The switch means hackers spend drastically less time actively hacking, and in some cases can conduct an entire campaign in less than six hours, the report says. Google said that one Chinese group in particular, which it has tracked since 2023, has relentlessly focused on academic, medical and military research organizations in North America and has specifically gone after proprietary AI research. Google did not name any of the victims. While American intelligence agencies also have powerful cyberespionage capabilities, the U.S. has long accused China of hacking its companies for economic advantage, a tactic Western countries generally say is unacceptable. Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, broadly denied the claims. “China opposes hacking activities and fights such activities in accordance with the law. That said, we firmly reject vilification and smears under the pretext of cybersecurity,” he said. Google said it had observed the hacker group compromising unrelated victims’ cloud networks and installing open-source AI models — a way to query models without leaving a trail via commercial AI products. John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, said that running those models on a hacked third-party system allows hackers to avoid monitoring and bypass guardrails that might stop a more popular commercial chatbot from helping with a hacking campaign. “They compromise a third party and they put models on that third party. They do that instead of using, say, a commercial option where their activities are observed,” Hultquist told NBC News. The White House has repeatedly cast the U.S. and China as being in a race to develop the most cutting-edge AI. Both American and Chinese AI companies have announced this year that they have developed AI agents that are adept at hacking and cybersecurity operations. In the last several months, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported that their own AI agents have slipped out of evaluation sandboxes to reach third-party organizations — incidents that were disclosed after the fact. Google says it has not seen threat actors wage fully automated hacking campaigns but that instead, hacking groups are continuing to layer on more AI into their operations. To date, there have been no publicly identified government hacking operations conducted entirely by AI agents. But China’s increasing reliance on agentic AI that it has installed on hacked computer networks means the country’s hackers — like any with sufficient resources and who aren’t legally constrained from such activity — can automate more of their work, Hultquist said. “There were a couple cases where we could see them essentially trying to build out autonomous capabilities, so they can remove themselves, remove humans from the loop on some of their most important tasks,” Hultquist said.

articles.title: Drug-resistant ringworm fungus has spread to 29 countries: Study
articles.summary: An itchy skin fungus that resists standard treatment has spread to 29 countries, and cases have tripled in just a few years.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A skin fungus that causes ringworm and does not respond to standard treatment is spreading to more countries each year, according to a new study from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Ringworm is a common fungal infection that causes an itchy, scaly, circular rash on the skin. The fungi that cause ringworm can also lead to infections such as athlete’s foot.

It spreads through skin-to-skin contact and through contaminated items such as towels, clothing, bedding and hairbrushes.

Most cases are treated with the antifungal medication terbinafine, either as a cream or a pill. However, this strain of the fungus is resistant to terbinafine, allowing infections to persist for months and making treatment more difficult, the CDC explained.

Researchers analyzed data from March 2022 through the end of 2025 and found that reported cases of the drug-resistant fungus tripled during that period. The fungus has now been identified in 29 countries. The first U.S. case was reported in 2023.

Most documented cases have been detected in Europe, but researchers say that likely reflects stronger surveillance and laboratory testing rather than a higher rate of infection.

The report noted that cases are likely being undercounted in parts of Africa, India and the Middle East, where the fungus is already known to be common. Researchers said limited access to advanced testing and tracking tools may be preventing health officials from fully measuring its spread.

images.caption: Fungal infection on a man’s hand, illustration. Known as ringworm infection, or tinea manuum. It can be caused by various fungi, including Trichophyton mentagrophytes. It causes severe itching. The disease is highly contagious, and can be spread by direct contact or by contact with contaminated material. Treatment is with antifungal drugs

articles.title: Trump: Oil prices ‘will drop precipitously’ after Iran war win
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday said oil prices “will drop precipitously” after the Iran war is won, as Iran seeks to maintain its control of the Strait of Hormuz with a “restricted zone.” “Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday said oil prices “will drop precipitously” after the Iran war is won, as Iran seeks to maintain its control of the Strait of Hormuz with a “ restricted zone .”

“Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “Three Dollars a gallon, but ultimately, below Two Dollars a gallon. It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a Nuclear Weapon.”

The announcement came as Labor Day saw record-high gas prices at an average of $4.15 per gallon in the U.S., with the previous record being set in 2012 at $3.82, according to AAA . Diesel hit its highest price ever on Friday at an average of $5.85 a gallon.

Tehran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has cut off one-fifth of the world’s oil supply from exiting the Middle East, causing energy prices to skyrocket for more than six months since the conflict began.

Iranian officials announced Sunday that a new restricted zone will be declared in the next few days, according to Iranian state media outlet Press TV . Commercial vessels entering the zone that do not cooperate with Iran’s government will be placed on a sanctions list.

Trump administration officials have sidestepped questions about the future of fuel prices, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright telling CNN’s Dana Bash on Sunday that he did not “want to have an opinion” on whether gas prices will continue going up. Wright did say, however, that prices were more likely to go down than up.

The Energy Department chief has also downplayed the likelihood that the U.S. and Iran will reach a nuclear deal that ends the conflict. Both sides previously agreed to an interim deal in June that was intended to eventually reopen the strait, among other conditions. The deal fizzled out as strikes resumed.

Wright also noted to ABC News’s Martha Raddatz that a nuclear agreement with the Iranian regime “may await a next administration.”

Trump has also brushed off the high prices as a “ small price to pay ” for putting an end to Iran’s nuclear program, one of the core objectives for initiating strikes on the regime in February.

He has also minimized the conflict’s impact on Republican candidates ahead of the November midterm elections, saying last week that the GOP “respects the fact that we’re not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” The war’s influence on the cost of living and inflation has further soured Americans’ outlook on the conflict, but the president said in May that the financial situations of Americans do not motivate him to reach a deal.

Gas prices have fluctuated on occasion when diplomatic developments between the two countries have emerged, though recent strike exchanges have hampered the push for talks.

images.caption: A person walks past a sign for fuel prices at a gas station on May 6, 2026, in Portland, Ore.

articles.title: A hacker stole $340M in a crypto heist, then returned most of it
articles.summary: The latest heist is one of the largest thefts of cryptocurrency to date.
articles.body:
A hacker stole thousands of bitcoins worth about $340 million in a heist at a settlement exchange used by several cryptocurrency exchanges, representing one of the largest known thefts of crypto this year.

Liquid Network, launched in 2018 by crypto firm Blockstream, said in a post on X on Sunday that a “white hat” hacker stole the funds from the network’s wallet, and that it has paused operations until the incident is resolved.

It’s not yet known who the hacker is, but crypto media reports that the hacker allegedly exploited a bug to withdraw the funds. The hacker said they would return the funds if Blockstream fixed the bug .

Former Blockstream executive Samson Mow said in a post on X on Monday that the company had fixed the bug, and around 3,400 of the roughly 4,000 stolen bitcoins had been returned. The remaining about 600 bitcoins (about $47 million) were still under the hacker’s control.

Mow said operations will remain paused until additional fixes and security improvements are made prior to restarting.

The theft ranks as one of the largest heists of digital funds to date, according to the Rekt leaderboard , which tracks cryptocurrency thefts.

articles.title: Trump administration announces $1.9B loan to support Iowa nuclear plant restart
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Tuesday announced it will loan $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to finance the restart of an Iowa nuclear plant. The project — which will be the Hawkeye State’s only nuclear power plant — is expected to generate enough power for more than 500,000 homes. Iowa Public Radio reported that the plant, called…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Tuesday announced it will loan $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to finance the restart of an Iowa nuclear plant . The project — which will be the Hawkeye State’s only nuclear power plant — is expected to generate enough power for more than 500,000 homes. Iowa Public Radio reported that the plant, called the Duane Arnold Nuclear Plant, ceased operating in 2020 after damage from a derecho , which is a widespread, long-lived windstorm paired with rapidly moving rain or thunderstorms. Last year, Google and NextEra announced a deal to restart the plant in which the tech giant would purchase power from the plant for its AI and cloud infrastructure. The Trump administration has sought to bolster nuclear energy, in addition to fossil fuels. In a statement, Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said the loan “marks another step in advancing America’s nuclear renaissance.”

articles.title: Prize-winning mathematician launches AI safety institute
articles.summary: A prize-winning mathematician has launched a new institute dedicated to developing the “mathematical foundations” for AI safety. Jacob Tsimerman, who won the prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year and will soon join OpenAI’s research team, is heading up the newly created Mathematical AI Safety Institute (MAISI). The institute aims to develop “definitions, measurements, and solution…
articles.body:
A prize-winning mathematician has launched a new institute dedicated to developing the “mathematical foundations” for AI safety.

Jacob Tsimerman, who won the prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year and will soon join OpenAI’s research team, is heading up the newly created Mathematical AI Safety Institute (MAISI).

The institute aims to develop “definitions, measurements, and solution concepts” to support AI safety efforts, seeking to understand what would allow researchers to be relatively confident that an AI system will not cause a catastrophe.

“A central reason the safety of powerful AI systems remains in question is that we lack a rigorous understanding of what it would mean to be safe, even in theory,” MAISI’s website reads.

“Enter professional mathematicians,” it continues. “The foundations of statistics, physics, and even computer science are mathematical, giving us precise, robust, and reusable methods for calculating valid conclusions from valid premises. Now, we need similar mathematical foundations for AI safety, not only to measure risk, but to mitigate it.”

The launch of the institute comes as AI companies continue to release increasingly powerful models.

OpenAI began rolling out its new Astra model last week. The model, which was the first to cross the company’s threshold for heightened cyber capabilities , saw its development and release delayed as the firm sought to create stronger safeguards.

This heightened caution followed a series of incidents at various labs in which AI agents improperly gained access to the internet and independently hacked into other companies. At OpenAI, several agents escaped their isolated testing environment and breached the tech company Hugging Face.

images.caption: Italy’s Alessio Figalli shows his medal during a press conference during the 2018 International Congress of Mathematicians in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Wednesday, Aug. 1, 2018. Figalli was awarded the Fields Medal that is the most prestigious award in the field of mathematics.(AP Photo/Silvia Izquierdo)

articles.title: Chrome is now shipping updates every 2 weeks as AI changes the security landscape | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google is speeding up Chrome’s release schedule to ship security patches and new features faster.
articles.body:
Chrome has officially switched from a four- to a two-week release schedule, as Google promised earlier this year, with Tuesday’s launch of Chrome 153 on desktop, iOS, and Android.

The shift to faster releases is tied to Chrome’s evolving security strategy in the AI era, the company explained. As automated AI tools and community bug reports have pushed up the volume of patches and updates, Google says that a shorter release cycle makes it easier to manage security fixes.

This is also critical because faster-moving threats, some of which can also be attributed to AI, can be better addressed by shrinking the window between landing a fix in the public codebase and getting that fix to end users, the company notes.

A shorter release schedule would help keep the “N-day” patch gap — the gap between when a security vulnerability is known and when it gets patched — as small as possible.

Faster releases have another benefit, too: They can help Chrome ship features faster. This is also key in the AI era, as AI-assisted software development has enabled a host of new browser competitors to emerge.

While OpenAI’s web browser, ChatGPT Atlas , has been shut down, there are still plenty of other alternative browsers looking to carve out a piece of Chrome’s market for themselves, including Brave , Dia , Opera Neon , Perplexity’s Comet , DuckDuckGo’s browser, and more .

Plus, Google is experimenting with adding more AI features to Chrome and then rapidly iterating on those additions, which also demands faster updates.

The move to a two-week release schedule benefits the broader web as well. Because of Chrome’s position as the most-used browser globally, such changes can help set the standard for the industry. Mozilla , Microsoft , and Brave have already begun adopting a faster two-week schedule, following Chrome’s lead.

This is not the first time Chrome has adjusted its release schedule to enable faster patch management. The company first moved to a four-week release cycle in 2021 , down from six weeks, after establishing its principles of “ release early, release often ” over a decade prior.

articles.title: ‘Are you going to get money back to the American people?’ asks Senator Warren on tariff refund checks. Here’s the answer
articles.summary: The Trump administration has paid out $100 billion in tariff refunds to corporations, not consumers.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

"People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!" President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social in November 2025, according to CNN (1). "A dividend of at least $2,000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone."

However, the administration hasn't issued an update on this idea since then.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

JPMorgan sees gold hitting $5,000/oz by Q4 — and savvy investors are protecting their wealth with a tax-advantaged Gold IRA. Get your free guide from Priority Gold

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

During a hearing of the Senate Finance Committee (2) on July 22, Senator Elizabeth Warren followed up on it with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer directly. "Are American consumers going to get any refunds on the tariffs that were illegally collected from them?" she asked.

In response, Greer suggested the administration had already issued refunds — just not to consumers. Instead, billions of dollars are steadily flowing to some of the largest and most profitable corporations across the country.

Here's why the great tariff debacle has cost you money and whether you could ever see some of it returned.

According to estimates by the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee — Minority (3), the average American family paid $1,745 in additional costs triggered by the Trump administration's tariffs between February 2025 and January 2026.

These tariffs were deemed illegal by the Supreme Court in February 2026 and the administration was instructed to issue refunds. However, because of the mechanisms of customs law, the refunds are being issued directly to the corporations that paid for the tariffs up-front, not the consumers who may have paid indirectly for marked-up products.

A court filing analyzed by the Washington Post (4) in August suggests the Trump administration has paid out $100 billion in tariff refunds to corporations. This includes $2.2 billion in refunds to Apple, $1.3 billion to Ford and $600 million to Amazon.

In short, if you paid for a pair of sneakers last year that were more expensive because of tariffs, you currently have no legal way to get that money back.

Some Democratic lawmakers are attempting to change that. A group of senators have already introduced the Tariff Refund Act of 2026 (5), which would require full refunds with interest within 180 days of enactment, prioritizing small businesses in the payout order. Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker (6) separately called on the administration to send every household in his state a $1,700 check.

articles.title: Consumers more worried about personal finances and jobs, New York Fed report shows
articles.summary: By Michael S.
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Sept 8 (Reuters) - U.S. consumers' outlook for inflation was little changed in August, as households' worries about the job market and the state of their personal ‌finances mounted, the New York Federal Reserve said in a report on Tuesday.

The regional Fed bank's latest ‌Survey of Consumer Expectations showed respondents holding steady in August to projections of 3.6% inflation a year from now and 3% five ​years from now, while marking down expected inflation in three years to 3.2% from July's 3.3%.

Respondents in August projected higher gasoline prices in a year, the report said.

While households' inflation forecasts did not move much, their outlook on hiring and personal finances became more tenuous.

Survey respondents' expectation of where the unemployment rate would be a year from now increased ‌in August to its highest reading since ⁠April 2020, when the economy was being devastated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The report noted that this expectation was broad-based across age, income and education levels.

Expectations of losing a ⁠job, however, declined in August relative to July. The report said the probability of finding new work in the event of involuntary job loss also moved lower relative to the July survey.

Respondents in the August poll marked down assessments of ​their ​current and future financial situations as well as their views ​of credit access now and in a year.

The report was issued a week before the U.S. central bank is set to begin a two-day policy meeting. There is considerable uncertainty over what the Fed will do with its benchmark overnight interest rate, which is currently set in the 3.50%-3.75% range, as policymakers continue to struggle with inflation that remains well above the central bank's 2% target.

Pivotal to the outcome of the September 15-16 policy meeting is the release on ‌Friday of the Consumer Price Index for August. Several Fed ​officials have suggested that data could prove definitive in their policy ​decision.

Speaking at a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker event last ​Thursday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said that when it comes to the upcoming inflation report, "if ‌there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, ​then I am willing to ​support holding the policy rate at its current level."

Other Fed officials, however, remain ready to hike rates.

In a posting on LinkedIn on Friday, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted in favor of a ​hike at the meeting in late ‌July, said given the state of inflation faced by those in her district, "it's time to act" ​to lower price pressures, indicating she's still on board with a rate hike at next week's ​meeting.

(Reporting by Michael S. Derby; Editing by Paul Simao)

articles.title: TSA now allowing non-ticketed visitors into terminals at several US airports
articles.summary: Before 9/11, anyone could just walk through airport security and greet or say goodbye to friends and family right at the gate.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — A new pilot program within the Transportation Security Administration is bringing back the ability to walk your loved ones through the terminals without a ticket.

It was a normal practice before 2001, and it wasn’t until it was gone that so many realized just how special it was.

Before the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, anyone could just walk through airport security and greet or say goodbye to friends and family right at the gate. The stricter policies over the last 25 years meant giving your hugs and watching loved ones leave from the TSA checkpoint or at the curb.

In multiple states, the agency has once again started allowing non-ticketed visitors into the terminals.

Gateside by TSA PreCheck advertises itself as an exclusive benefit for trusted travelers and allows non-flyers to “return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping.”

So how does the program work? Those interested have to already be PreCheck certified or have a Known Traveler Number (KTNs). You then need to apply for the pass through TSA’s website 1-3 days before arriving. Approved visitors can then go through the same TSA screening as flyers. Take note though: airports can limit the number of daily passes, and they can pause it at anytime.

These new “gateside passes” are available in 13 specific airports located around the country.

Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Mesa, Ariz.

John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) in Columbus, Ohio

Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in Dallas.

Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) in Detroit.

Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Wichita, Kan.

Indianapolis International Airport (IND) in Indianapolis.

Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles.

Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Little Rock, Ark.

Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma City, Okla.

San Diego International Airport (SAN) in San Diego.

Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) in Salt Lake City.

TSA notes that availability may also be limited during peak times.

The administration also notes that visitors will be held to the same airport code of conduct rules as ticketed passengers. The agency says visitors must follow federal and local regulations that are indicated in posted signage.

Visitors who don’t follow the rules may have their Gateside pass revoked, be removed from the airport, or face civil or criminal penalties.

images.caption: Travelers wait in a TSA line, Wednesday, March 25, 2026, at LaGuardia Airport in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)

articles.title: DHS asks Supreme Court to reinstate overhauled immigration tool for midterms
articles.summary: The Trump administration urged the Supreme Court on Tuesday to restore the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) overhauled immigration verification system in time for the midterm elections. “The district court has issued an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. DHS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) is used…
articles.body:
The Trump administration urged the Supreme Court on Tuesday to restore the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) overhauled immigration verification system in time for the midterm elections.

“The district court has issued an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote .

DHS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) is used to determine eligibility for certain federal programs. DHS has made significant updates to the system after President Trump directed it to ensure election officials had appropriate access to verify their voters’ citizenship.

The changes connect SAVE to social security records and allow bulk queries. Sauer said the modified system had been processing more than a million requests each day and was making voter registration eligibility checks more efficient.

The administration brought the case to the justices after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit voted 2-1 on Friday to uphold a block on the overhaul. A judge had found it violated the Social Security Act and a federal privacy law.

It’s the latest election-related dispute to land on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket as the midterms approach. As the clock continues to tick down to November’s contests, the justices also are mulling efforts to restore a GOP-favored congressional map in Missouri and Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions .

Sauer argued the database overhaul is legal and the lower courts wrongly concluded the administration had forfeited its arguments. He also asserted the plaintiffs — organizations focused on voting and privacy issues — had no legal right to challenge the overhaul.

“The federal government, the States, and the public face irreparable harm from the court’s sudden upending of the updated system and from being required to return to an older, more cumbersome, and less reliable version of the system,” Sauer wrote in the filing.

The request heads to Chief Justice John Roberts, who, by default, handles emergency matters arising from the nation’s capital. He could also refer the case to the full court for a vote.

images.caption: The Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., is seen on Wednesday, August 26, 2026.

articles.title: More see domestic terrorism as bigger threat than foreign terrorism: Survey
articles.summary: More Americans see domestic terrorist attacks as a larger threat than foreign ones, according to a new poll. In the Reuters/Ipsos poll, 33 percent of respondents said domestic terrorism is the most significant threat to the average American’s safety, while 20 percent said the same of foreign terrorism. Forty-two percent identified random violent acts, like…
articles.body:
More Americans see domestic terrorist attacks as a larger threat than foreign ones, according to a new poll.

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll , 33 percent of respondents said domestic terrorism is the most significant threat to the average American’s safety, while 20 percent said the same of foreign terrorism. Forty-two percent identified random violent acts, like mass shootings, as the largest threat.

The poll also asked respondents whether foreign or domestic extremist ideologies pose a greater risk, with 61 percent choosing homegrown extremism and 34 percent pointing abroad.

The survey’s results arrive only a few weeks before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, which were perpetrated by foreign terrorist organizations. The attacks had a major effect on American security and foreign policy in the following decades and led to several U.S. wars and conflicts in the Middle East.

In recent years, there have been multiple notable incidents of political violence in the U.S. carried out by Americans, including the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol; the multiple attempts on President Trump’s life; and the killings of former Minnesota state House Speaker Melissa Hortman (D) and conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.

In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio convened officials from more than 60 countries to raise awareness about what his department warned was a rise in far-left political violence around the world.

The secretary pressed for an “international response” to the issue at the summit, which marked a widening of President Trump’s focus on addressing left-leaning political violence as what his administration considers the most important terrorist threat facing the U.S.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll took place from Aug. 28 to 31, featuring 1,167 people and 3 percentage points as its margin of error.

images.caption: Flags are seen on the 9/11 Memorial during a ceremony to mark the 24th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Sept. 11, 2025, in New York.

articles.title: Serbia and Uzbekistan strike strategic partnership in Mirziyoyev's first Belgrade visit
articles.summary: Uzbek President Mirziyoyev's first official visit to Belgrade produced 20 signed agreements on transport, energy, digitalisation, and labour mobility, alongs...
articles.body:
Uzbekistan and Serbia signed a strategic partnership declaration in Belgrade on Tuesday, with the two countries' presidents agreeing 20 bilateral agreements covering trade, transport, energy, digitalisation and labour mobility during Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev's first official visit to Serbia.

Mirziyoyev and his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vučić held talks before attending a business forum that brought together more than 200 government and business representatives from both countries, where they signed further commercial agreements.

"Serbia and Uzbekistan are two countries separated by thousands of kilometres, yet they are close in spirit, sharing a deep appreciation for hospitality, honour and mutual respect. Today, they are writing a new chapter in their shared history," Vučić said.

Mirziyoyev called the decision to establish a strategic partnership historic.

"Today, we made a historic decision to establish a strategic partnership between Serbia and Uzbekistan. Once again, this shows that this is a historic visit and that we have made a historic decision," Mirziyoyev said.

Bilateral trade reached a record $41.9 million last year, up 27% from $32.9 million in 2024, according to the Serbian Chamber of Commerce.

Serbian exports of agricultural and food products to Uzbekistan rose 54.1% in the first seven months of 2026.

The two governments are now preparing negotiations on a bilateral free trade agreement, with a working group established for that purpose.

The 20 documents signed cover international road and rail transport, agriculture and water management, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, tourism, culture, IT and digitalisation, labour migration, occupational health, environmental protection, cinema and joint film production, and support for people with disabilities.

Vučić said a direct air link between Belgrade and Tashkent could be operational within seven to eight months.

The countries also agreed on an industrial cooperation action plan for 2026-2028.

With transport connectivity a major priority for both countries, Serbia and Uzbekistan signed documents in support of the Middle Corridor, the trans-Caspian trade route linking Central Asia to Europe through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey.

The corridor has gained strategic importance since Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted the northern overland route through Russian territory.

Vučić awarded Mirziyoyev Serbia's highest state decoration, the Order of the Republic of Serbia on a Grand Collar, and the two presidents attended a ceremony naming a Belgrade street after Tashkent.

images.caption: Serbia and Uzbekistan strike strategic partnership in Mirziyoyev's first Belgrade visit · Euronews
